attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post, giving his verdict on the TED2023 talks.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'so far' and 'seem to'. It joins a hedged comparison ('seem to have been best calibrated') with a firm causal claim (LLM bugs stymied Khanmigo and the pin). Under policy, the hedged comparison is not scored. Only the bugs claim is firm.

contract.note: The contract requires the hedged 'seem to have been best calibrated' comparison to be established before the claim can be supported. Policy says hedged language is not scored. Its reading of 'stymied' as materially hindered is fair. Its requirement to separate model errors from other failures is reasonable.

evidence.note: CNN's firsthand test in August 2023, inside the period: Khanmigo's calculation errors hindered its tutoring. It also notes the product's coaching strengths.
Inverse's review of 11 April 2024 documents hallucinations in the pin's Vision feature. It also credits functions that worked and names non-LLM failures, so it only partly backs 'stymied'.
Secondary account, dated February 2024, of the WSJ test, which found frequent arithmetic errors in Khanmigo. The pilot was still running.
TED's own record of what the speakers said. It does not establish which speakers proved better calibrated.

reviews.rationale: The evidence supports model errors hindering Khanmigo. It partly supports the same for the Humane pin, though the pin's review also cites non-LLM problems. The comparative calibration part is hedged and was never evaluated: the packet makes no comparison of the speakers. Under the contract the whole proposition is therefore not settled. The bugs part on its own leans supported.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: The wording is faithful, but this is an aphorism used to stress why tutor hallucinations matter, not a testable causal law. 'Can't teach' is rhetorical emphasis.

contract.note: The contract reads the maxim as a categorical causal claim, measured by learner uncertainty and learning gains. Marcus supplied neither measure, and reading 'can't' as strict impossibility stretches it against him.

evidence.note: A 2025 randomised trial found learning even with feedback that was all wrong. It did not establish that learners were unsure what to believe.
2026 preprint, published before the evaluation date. It tested a warning that the tutor might make mistakes, with no actual errors, and reports no learning gains.

reviews.rationale: This is a rhetorical maxim with no defined measure, not a testable claim. Even taken literally, the packet's studies do not measure learner uncertainty together with learning gains, so they could not settle it.

attribution.note: Marcus's own observation in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'some genuine progress' and 'especially led by the UN and the Council of Europe'. Dropping his statement about his own advocacy is fine.

contract.note: Counting concrete multilateral milestones at both bodies as 'progress' is an ordinary, fair reading of his words. The window, from April 2023 to the post, fits his comparison with the previous TED.

evidence.note: The UN's own account says the General Assembly adopted an AI resolution without a vote in March 2024, inside the window.
Official Council of Europe record: on 14 March 2024 its AI committee approved the draft Framework Convention and sent it on for formal adoption.

reviews.rationale: Official records show concrete AI-governance milestones at both bodies before 15 April 2024. The UN General Assembly adopted an AI resolution, and the Council of Europe's AI committee approved its draft convention. Together these meet the contract's test for genuine progress led by the UN and the Council of Europe.

attribution.note: The description of Choi's worry is a paraphrase, but 'They still aren't' is Marcus's own assertion.

semantics.note: Faithful: an observation that LLMs were still unreliable around April 2024.

contract.note: Reading 'unreliable' as recurring errors that stop users relying on answers without checking is ordinary and fair. The January to March 2024 window is reasonable.

evidence.note: March 2024 benchmark of 13 models from four families finds recurring factual errors in long-form answers. Larger models did better.
February 2024 human annotations find substantial hallucination in dialogue summaries, whatever the model's size.

reviews.rationale: Two evaluations from within the window, covering several model families and different tasks, document recurring factual errors. That meets the support condition. Better results from larger models show improvement, not reliability.
